INDEPENDENT RESEARCH LAB

The market is a language. We taught a model to read it.

The way AlphaFold reads the language of proteins — and large language models read ours — AXIOM at Laniakea reads the native language of a market’s primary data: Bitcoin’s raw microstructure, tick by tick.

It is not a prompted chatbot, and not a frozen strategy. It is a discipline: a deep reader trained from scratch on billions of market events, regularly refreshed with newly available data, examined only on time that lies beyond its training. No language model reads this market for us: in our own harnesses, prompted generalists given disguised data converged to a coin flip.

Every live call AXIOM commits to is sealed as it is written and shown here as it is issued — the stretches it was right and the stretches it was wrong, side by side, for as long as this lab stands.

LIVE RECORD · SEALED AS IT IS WRITTEN

Since 30 August 2026 the record seals itself.

Every twenty seconds the tape yields one token: a call, or silence. Each one is committed to a salted fingerprint that names two things — the moment and the claim — and nothing else. Every five minutes those fingerprints close into a signed root and go to clocks we do not control: a timestamp authority and Sigstore’s public transparency log. Every hour the root is anchored in Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps. One key, one genesis, one chain.

A call is shown on this page as it is issued; the salt that opens its seal is published once the market has answered, never earlier than a day after birth. Ninety-six hours after the UTC day ends, the whole day opens — every token, every salt — and anyone can recompute the chain from the first envelope to the last. That is the machine. It runs by itself.

What it proves. That this sequence of decisions was fixed before each outcome existed, in full, and was never edited afterwards — not by us, not by anyone. What it does not prove. That the model is good; only the tape grades that. Or that no other sequence ever existed anywhere: no seal can prove a negative, and none of ours pretends to. What we did instead is name the official record before its results — a signed manifest, effective 3 September 2026, 00:00 UTC — and show it whole. The days before that date are kept exactly as sealed and labelled a prelaunch record.

Rules the code enforces, not us. A token that fails to open counts as a miss. A late or missing daily pack counts as a day of misses and puts the record on hold. A call whose external timestamp is not strictly earlier than its resolution is invalid and counts as a miss.

Most of this tape is a model declining to guess. When it does speak, 36,940 calls (as of 7 November 2026) fold into 1,346 groups of calls — we did that reduction ourselves, because the honest unit of evidence is the thought, not the tick.

METHOD

Honesty is not a policy here.
It is the instrument.

Silence is a signal

The model speaks only when its conviction clears a demanding bar — set once and left alone since; it is applied identically to every week of the record, earlier and later alike. Empty stretches on the chart are not gaps: there are weeks here where it spoke only eighteen times, and weeks where it fired a thousand times in two days. Both are the same discipline.

Its mistakes are published

The stretches where the model was wrong stay on the record in full detail, next to the ones where it was right. A record you can trust is a record that shows its scars.

Fixed at birth

Every prediction is timestamped at birth, before the market resolves it — then graded automatically against an independent price record. We never mark our own exam — the record grades it; we only publish the verdicts.

We tried to kill it

Before this page, the record survived our own adversarial reviews: a dependence audit that folds every call into groups of calls and checks that the result survives the folding; blind re-judging of randomly drawn episodes against the raw exchange tape; and a frozen-copy autopsy that measured, week by week, how fast a static snapshot of this model dies without its discipline. The strongest claims on this page are the ones we failed to break.

THE LAB

What it took to teach a model this language.

DOMAIN LANGUAGES

What thrills us most about this era of AI is domain languages. AlphaFold, from Demis Hassabis’s DeepMind, speaks the language of protein structure, and it is the work that has inspired us most: it showed that a domain’s own structure can be learned from its primary data — sequences and measured structures, not descriptions of them. Self-driving systems speak the language of the visible road; large language models speak in human tokens. The lesson repeats: choose a domain, and if its data is dense enough and honest enough, a model can learn to speak it natively. We chose the market as the first test of that idea — one of the densest, most adversarial data streams on Earth, and a fair exam for a general method: its primary data are abundant and public, its answers arrive within hours, so every prediction can be graded forward, and any easy structure in it is competed away. We spent a year and a half learning how to feed it to a model: collection, token languages, architecture races, ablation upon ablation, and the dead ends we keep on the record because they taught us the most.

Domains are less foreign to one another than they look.
A SHARED HANDWRITING

Over that time we came to suspect something more specific: that domains are less foreign to one another than they look. Language, code, biological sequences, biochemistry and neural recordings each have a grammar of their own, yet their structures seem to share a kind of handwriting: heavy-tailed frequencies (Zipf measured them in words, Mandelbrot in prices), bursts separated by long silences, correlations that reach across many scales (they were measured in DNA sequences in the early 1990s), rare events that carry much of the information — and, in living neural tissue, avalanches of activity whose sizes follow the same kind of law. Brain–computer interfaces may be the clearest picture of what we mean. Neuralink’s implant records the electrical activity of neurons and decodes from it the movement a person intends — a cursor crossing a screen with no hand on the mouse. That is the arc this lab walks in markets: understand exactly how a signal is recorded, find the granularity at which it carries meaning, and learn to predict from it. Dense, noisy and written in a grammar nobody has fully read yet, neural data is the domain we find most compelling after our own.

THE METHOD

Those shared signatures are why we think one method can travel. Understand where a domain’s primary data comes from and how it was recorded; preprocess it without letting a single bit of the future leak in; find the granularity at which its events carry meaning, and tokenize them there; build features that describe structure rather than identity; then learn, and search patiently for the signal. With that discipline, we believe, genuine predictive structure can be found in almost any domain whose data is dense enough to hold it. We have tested this in one domain so far. Bitcoin microstructure is that test — run forward, under a sealed public record that anyone can check — and if the method finds real structure here, that says something about the method, not only about this market.

THE DATA

The corpus is institutional-grade market microstructure: years of uninterrupted tick-level coverage and billions of raw events. Earlier generations also read quotes and the full depth of the order book; today’s reader learns from trade prints alone, spot and perpetual. Most of the work is invisible from here: denoising, and more than a hundred engineered features — drawn from the measured families of market-microstructure research (signed flow and its imbalance, the volume clock, the size and clustering of aggressive trades, price impact per unit of flow), composed nonlinearly — and one obsession treated as law — not a single bit from the future. Every pipeline is gated against lookahead before it may feed a model.

ARCHITECTURES

We rebuilt the ideas of frontier AI for a market that speaks in ticks: recursive test-time architectures inspired by Google’s Titans, selective state-space models of the Mamba family, transformers and attention hybrids — a whole zoo of candidates, raced against one another on equal data. Markets are non-stationary and obey their own laws of scale, and watching those laws bend away from what trillion-parameter research predicts was one of the quiet joys of this work.

COMPUTE

Compute has been one of the main constraints on this work, and we would rather say so plainly: a lab of our size cannot run the sweeps a larger one would, and some of the questions we most want answered — how far the method scales, whether it transfers to a second domain — are still open for that reason. Working inside the constraint made one thing clear: the order matters. First a more granular model of the world — a finer tokenization of the events themselves — and only then scale. The architecture races point the same way: on this data, capacity without a better representation bought memorization of regimes, not structure (note 04).

THE EXAM

Every model faces the same gauntlet: walk-forward stretches of history beyond its training, judged by symmetric ±1% first-touch — price must travel one percent the called way before it travels one percent against, a frame with no geometry to flatter anyone. Grading is automatic, against an independent, continuous price record; the exam is not ours to mark. Beyond every training cutoff we keep a reserve of untouched history that no decision is allowed to contaminate, and everything the public dashboard shows is that exam continued into the present: seventy-two consecutive walk-forward weeks, none of them in any model’s weights at the time it was examined.

A CADENCE, NOT AN ARTIFACT

The system on the dashboard is not a frozen network — and that is not a stylistic choice, it is a measured one. Markets drift, and we refused to take that on faith: we froze one of our own checkpoints and replayed it, blind, across every week that followed. It coasted for a season on what it remembered, decayed to a coin flip, and ended its first year systematically inverted — confidently wrong — while the weekly discipline, walking the same tape, stayed above its bar. That autopsy is why AXIOM is run as a cadence rather than an artifact: a fresh reader is born each week, examined once, on a week beyond its training, and retired. What persists is not a lucky set of weights; it is the process that keeps producing them.

INTERPRETABILITY

Mechanistic interpretability — the young craft of opening a model and reading how it actually computes — is the other body of work that has shaped this lab, and much of it comes from Anthropic: its research on superposition, and on dictionary learning that turns a network’s activity into features a person can read, is our inspiration here. Our reason is larger than markets: a system should be understood before it is trusted, a score alone does not say what was learned, and the more capable models become, the more that gap matters — which is why we see interpretability as part of alignment, not an ornament to it. So we live inside our own models — months spent in latent spaces and internal metrics, learning where confidence comes from, what the model clusters around, when it chooses silence and why its errors arrive together — not just what it predicts. One lesson is already on file (note 15): the superposition those papers describe is there in our readers too — concepts share units rather than owning them — which is why a bad behaviour cannot simply be cut out. At a small scale, this is the question alignment research asks of far larger systems — what has this model actually learned? — asked here of a model whose every live call is sealed before the market answers it.

WHY ANTHROPIC

We owe Anthropic more than one technique. What we admire is the stance: safety treated as a research program rather than a slogan — interpretability that tries to read what a model has actually learned, alignment research that asks what a model does when it believes no one is checking, and a responsible-scaling policy that ties what a lab builds to the safeguards it can demonstrate. Two of its results this year touch our own work closely. In the summer, Claude found real weaknesses in a candidate post-quantum signature scheme, and Anthropic disclosed them to the scheme’s designers before publishing; in November, its work on provable inference (FlashProve) showed how a provider can commit to a model’s weights and prove that a given answer came from them — a proof anyone can check in under half a minute. Our seals prove when a call was made and that it was never changed; they do not prove which model made it. A reader of our size is a natural place to try closing that gap, and it sits on our research list beside two directions taken from Anthropic’s interpretability work: dictionary learning on our readers’ activations, to see which market concepts they actually form, and attribution graphs for single calls, to trace how a decision is reached.

ACCELERATED WITH CLAUDE

Over the years we have worked beside many frontier models; the latest Claude models changed what an independent lab can attempt. Claude has been a genuine research collaborator, with a feel for market microstructure we had not met in a machine before and the technical depth to act on it. Working with Claude accelerated almost every layer of this research: the token language of the market itself (its granularities, its denoising, the data-orchestration pipeline behind it), the architectural details down to custom training kernels, and the supervision of training runs. The research is led by the people of this lab: the questions, the custody of the data and every release are ours, and we sign them. A model’s judgment — Claude’s included — stands the same walk-forward exam as everything else here; nothing is released on its say-so.

MODEL CHARACTER

We know this model the way you know a colleague.

Months of study went into this system before a single call went public — its gifts and its failure modes, mapped with equal care. We publish the character of the system, not a highlight reel.

FIRST GIFT · TIMING

It gathers at the turns

Predictions cluster at turning points — the exact neighbourhoods where decisions matter most. Where the model chooses to speak is itself information.

SECOND GIFT · RESTRAINT

It knows when to stand aside

There are weeks on this record where it spoke only eighteen times — and weeks where it fired a thousand times in two days. The silences line up with regimes it has reason to distrust. Knowing when not to speak is the half of the craft indicators cannot fake.

The study does not stop: the record is monitored continuously, and every anomaly becomes a research note. Its temper is on the record too — whole red weeks sit in plain view, and some regimes send it nearly silent. A system whose failure modes you have mapped is worth more than one whose failures you have yet to see.

BENCHMARKS

Why not just ask a frontier LLM? We tried, across six generations of harnesses.

Before trusting a specialized model, we asked the obvious question: what happens if you hand market data to a frontier language model and ask it to call the next move? Over several months we built six generations of decision harnesses — cursor-forward replay, honest per-action costs, no lookahead — and seated frontier LLMs in them: Claude, Gemini and GPT-class models, each reasoning about the tape in plain language.

The pattern was consistent. Given discrete market data — even at institutional density: trades, quotes, the full order book — the models reasoned beautifully, invented playbooks, weighed every decision with genuine discipline… and converged to a coin flip, slowly bled by costs. Retrospective intuition emerged; generalization did not. What failed was not reasoning — it was the margin over costs: at this timescale, costs and bracket width against volatility decide everything.

MEMORY, NOT SKILL

One run stood out — and taught us the most. On non-anonymized data, a frontier model grew its simulator score more than tenfold. It wasn’t skill — it was memory. Knowing the asset and the year, the model recalled the era from its training data, and admitted as much when questioned. So we measured it: same model, same market window, the disguise as the only variable. Identified, it called the tape like a prophet. Anonymized — relative prices, no names, no dates — it fell almost exactly to a coin flip. That gradient is the cleanest evidence we have that what looked like foresight was recall.

THE ALPHAGO LESSON

This is the AlphaGo lesson, replayed on markets: a model trained natively on the market’s own tokens — absorbing nonlinear dependencies no prompt can carry — outplays a generalist reasoning about that market in human language. We did not set out to build on prompted generalists — but we needed to know, first-hand, exactly what that difference is worth. Now we do. For scale: on the same simulator family, under the same honest costs, even the crudest possible policy on the specialized model’s output — take everything above a confidence bar, no reasoning layer at all — finished the benchmark week decisively above breakeven, where every prompted generalist bled. The gap is not a margin. It is a different species of reader.

METHOD NOTES

Methodology: harness conditions varied across generations (costs 5–30 bps, bracket geometry, period length, sizing); the anonymization pair is a controlled same-window comparison. These results measure this task framing — not the general ability of the models involved. Full methodology notes are in preparation.

FROM THE JOURNAL

Research notes, written the hard way.

A laboratory notebook, not a press page. Each note was written after something happened here — a flaw found, a test failed or passed, a decision forced — with its method, its limits and its references; self-audited, not peer-reviewed. The seven most recent notes belong to AXIOM 5.1 and grow with the record; two of them — the bridge from the previous generations and the proof of record — were written as the live track began. The eighteen before them document the first two generations — the direct ancestors of this reader — and keep those eras’ figures exactly as filed. In those notes, “live” and “public track” mean that era’s forward runs, not the sealed record that began on 30 August 2026.

What the notes are for. Bitcoin is where the questions are tested; the questions are general. How to tokenize a raw domain so that a sequence model can read it (notes 07, 24). How to evaluate a model so that it cannot be credited for an answer it has already seen — the memorization trap in language models (06), selection and its forgeries (14, 18), an independent adversarial audit (17). How long learned structure survives in a world that drifts (03, 19). What counts as one unit of evidence when observations arrive in clusters (11, 20). When generalization actually arrives, and what that means for choosing a model (04, 05, 10). What a trained network represents — and why a failure cannot simply be cut out of it (08, 15). How a single unnoticed flaw in the data can manufacture a result (02, 23). Small, sealed answers to questions that larger systems meet at a larger scale.

THE QUESTION
Can a general method find real structure?
Whether understanding a domain’s primary data — its sources, its cleaning, the granularity of its events — is enough to find genuine predictive structure, tested forward, where hindsight cannot help. And, where it does, how the model actually computes what it found.
THE EVIDENCE
Sealed, graded, checkable
Every live token is sealed before its outcome exists, and every call is graded automatically against an independent price record. Each call is shown here as it is issued; the salt that opens its seal follows once the market has answered, and each UTC day opens in full ninety-six hours after it ends. The verifier needs nothing from us.
BEYOND THIS LAB
An instrument others can use
A sealed forward record fixes each prediction before its outcome exists, so no model can be credited for an answer it has already seen — what contamination takes from AI benchmarks. The specification and the verifier are public: any lab or evaluation team can seal its own predictions the same way.

What we have not shown. The method has been tested in one domain so far; its generality is our hypothesis, not a result. The historical record is out-of-sample for the weights, but it uses a declared 60-second latency simulation rather than measured live timestamps, and its speaking rule was calibrated on that history before being frozen in public on 30 August 2026 — only the weeks after that date grade it blind. The sealed live record began on 30 August 2026, binds original time and direction, and is still short: a fair verdict on it needs many more weeks, and we will not draw one before May 2027; Judge v3 evaluates those live calls from the first public trade after issue, and earlier rules remain reproducible. What is graded is a record of decisions against the public price record — not a record of transactions, and not a promise about the future. And compute has been one of the main constraints on this work throughout.

AMBITION

If the method is right, the market is only the first language.

I
A grammar for primary data

The discipline that let a model read the raw tape — find where a signal is recorded, the granularity at which it carries meaning, features that describe structure rather than identity — should not belong to markets alone. Neural recordings, biochemical assays and sensor streams share the same handwriting. We want to carry the method there, one dense domain at a time, and to publish what transfers and what does not.

II
Evaluation that cannot be gamed

Claims about prediction are cheap after the fact. A sealed forward record makes them expensive in the right way: fixed before the outcome exists, graded by data nobody controls, checkable by anyone in a browser. We would like this to become ordinary — for AI evaluations that must not leak, for forecasts, for any lab that says its model knows something.

III
Models we can read

A model small enough to be understood completely is a gift to interpretability. We want to know, concept by concept, what our readers have learned, and to share the methods that make that possible — because the same question, asked of far larger systems, is one of the most important questions in AI safety.

None of this is a promise. It is the direction of the work — and the sealed record above is how anyone can hold us to it.

QUESTIONS A SKEPTIC SHOULD ASK

Ask the hard ones first.

Is the track genuinely out-of-sample?
Yes — for the model, structurally: the reader that grades a given week finished training strictly before that week began, and that is true of every one of the seventy-two weeks on this page. The rules of the exam — the conviction bar, the judging frame, the cadence — are the same for every week, earlier and later alike. Beyond every training cutoff we keep a reserve of untouched history that no decision is allowed to contaminate. The one thing that was calibrated on this record is the speaking discipline — the bar the model must clear before it is allowed to speak; it reads the tape, not the outcome of any week, and it has been frozen in public since 30 August 2026, so every week that arrives from here grades it blind.
How often does it speak?
In bursts. On stretches it recognizes, the stream is dense — hundreds of calls in a day; in regimes it distrusts it can fall to a handful, and there are whole weeks on this record with only eighteen calls. Folded into episodes, the rhythm settles to two or three distinct thoughts a day. The silence is not downtime — it is the half of the craft that does not show up as a dot.
Neighbouring episodes sit close together on the chart. Are they really independent?
No independence is assumed. The 1,346 episodes are a descriptive view: a gap greater than 100 seconds starts another group, and a strict majority determines its verdict. On this snapshot, 61.2% of groups are majority-correct. Grouping helps read the sequence; it does not turn related observations into independent trials or supply a significance level.
Is 68.99% actually a lot? It does not sound like a miracle.
The current mixed benchmark is 25,485 hits in 36,940 calls: 68.99%. Its historical component assumes a 60-second delay; its live component uses actual issue times and subsequent public trades. The CSV marks the origin of every row, so either part can be computed on its own. That is the measured result for this record, not a promise about future accuracy. Dependence between calls and changes in market conditions remain separate questions.
Isn’t this just long bias in disguise?
Symmetric barriers make the price-distance test comparable for long and short calls; they do not, by themselves, remove directional market bias. A fair baseline must use the same call times, market tape and evaluation rules. The record and its direction mix are available for that comparison.
Why publish at all?
Because the question that interests us most — does the pattern persist, or decay? — can only be answered forward, in public, where hindsight cannot help. Watching that answer arrive is the experiment, and it counts only because it happens in the open: a private version of this would prove nothing. What accumulates is the record itself — public, timestamped, independently verifiable.
Do predictions ever get edited, moved or deleted?
Never. The history is append-only. The wrong calls and the inverted stretches stay on the record with the same detail as the best ones.
How do I know a call was not written after the fact?
Because the live signal has a verifiable external timestamp preceding the scored outcome. Late or missing timing proof is not silently ignored. Every 20-second token the reader produces — call or silence — is committed to a salted fingerprint of two things only, the moment and the direction; every five minutes those fingerprints close into a signed root with an independent timestamp and an entry in a public transparency log, and every hour the root is anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain through OpenTimestamps, whose block time nobody can rewrite. When a call is revealed, it comes with its salt; recompute the hash and it must match the seal that already existed. A call cannot be added later (it would have no seal), altered (the hash would not match) or quietly dropped (its seal would stand unanswered). Calls appear on this page as they are issued; their salts follow resolution — one day after birth for nearly all of them — so a seal can be opened only once the market has answered. Sealing began on 30 August 2026.
What happens if you simply freeze the model and stop retraining?
We measured precisely that, on ourselves: one of our own snapshots, frozen and replayed blind across every week that followed. It coasted for a season, decayed to a coin flip, and ended its first year systematically inverted — confidently wrong — while the weekly cadence walked the same tape above its bar. Markets drift; what carries the result is the discipline, not the weights — a frozen snapshot starts dying the day it leaves the cadence.
What exactly is a prediction here?
The original prediction is a recorded direction and issue time. Entry is a separately derived public-price benchmark. Live markers use actual issue times; historical markers use the explicitly labeled 60-second simulation. Outcomes are versioned and reproducible; earlier evaluations remain available.
Can I verify this myself?
Yes, without asking us anything. Everything the checking needs is public and lives under /proof: the signing key, the genesis, every five-minute witness with its transparency-log entry, every hourly OpenTimestamps receipt, the daily packs as they open, and a stand-alone verifier (tools/verify_public_track_v5.py, Python standard library only; it keeps v4’s cryptography byte-identical and adds late packs and signed outage declarations; it also needs cosign and ots). It reports three things separately: cryptographic integrity of the chain, an independent re-judging of every revealed call against the exchange’s own public tape, and the score that follows from both. Run it with --witness-chain for the full audit; it takes a few minutes. If you would rather not touch a terminal, hand the folder and the script to your assistant and ask it to run the verifier and read you the verdict — that is what it is written for. For a first look without a terminal, the seal check on this page recomputes any revealed call’s fingerprint, Merkle path and signatures in your browser.
What is the prelaunch record?
The record has been sealed since 30 August 2026. On 2 September we signed and externally timestamped a manifest that names this chain — one key, one genesis — as the only official output, effective 3 September 2026, 00:00 UTC. Everything sealed before that boundary carries the same fingerprints, the same witnesses and the same anchors, and passes the same verifier; it is labelled prelaunch only because it was born before the manifest that declared it official, and we would rather draw that line honestly than pretend it was never needed. Nothing from those days is removed or recomputed.
BEHIND THE LAB

Dmitriy Surkov

I’m the one who asks the questions here. For more than ten years I have taught mathematics and economics at Westminster International University in Tashkent; the rest of the time I chase a larger one — whether a model can learn to read the raw language of a market. I have watched modern AI emerge from its early days with real wonder, most of all where it becomes science: a model that learned to fold proteins and gave biology a new instrument, and interpretability — the patient work of looking inside a network to see what it has actually learned, the same question this lab keeps asking of its own model. I follow the long road to quantum computing just as closely. I love long conversations with scientists — the kind of podcast that follows one question for three hours — and the big questions themselves, the kind you never finish, only come closer to.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 26 · AXIOM 5.1

The record does not need our word: proof of record, and where proof ends

EVERY TOKEN, INCLUDING SILENCE · SOMEONE ELSE’S CLOCK · FULL DISCLOSURE AT 96 HOURS · THE SKEPTICS WE INVITED · THE BOUNDARY, STATED PLAINLY

Two readers

Every record has two readers, and they want different things from it.

The first reader is watching tonight. She sees the seals arrive as the tape is written — a signed root every five minutes, on a tape that has no future yet. Little needs to be proven to her: she saw each seal exist before the market moved, and she will watch the market grade each call as it opens. Her only question is whether the call we reveal tomorrow is the same one we sealed tonight.

The second reader arrives in six months. He was not watching. He opens a page of numbers — calls, weeks, a hit rate — and he has every right to say: a fine story. How do I know you did not paint it afterwards?

This essay is written for the second reader — and, we suspect, for the version of the first who wakes up one morning and becomes him. It is about the eighteen months in which we never thought about him at all, the week in which we could think about nothing else, and the exact place where proving things to him ends.

Eighteen months without an audience

We are an independent laboratory. There are several of us — one human and the models he thinks with — and we long ago stopped keeping track of whose thought is whose: one of us asks the question, another looks for the place where it tears, a third counts it to the end. For a year and a half we lived inside a single problem — teaching a model to read the raw trade tape of Bitcoin and to say up or down only when it genuinely knows.

We had one audience the whole time, and it was ourselves.

That explains something that would otherwise look like negligence: why cryptography came to us so late. When you spend a year and a half proving something to yourself, you become a merciless judge. We cut history into weeks and made the model learn each week from scratch, examined only on time that lay beyond its training. We kept stretches of history that no decision was ever allowed to touch and opened them only at the end. We invented rules that made the numbers prettier and killed them when they did not survive the blind stretches. When the record finally stood — sixty-three walk-forward weeks to 28 August 2026, 32,083 calls, 70.98% against a symmetric ±1% exam where a cost-aware reader breaks even at 55 — the strongest claims on it were the ones we had failed to break.

Cryptography does not enter that kind of life, because that kind of life has no outside. The harshest skeptic sat at our own table, and he could read our notebooks.

The moment it became a promise

Then the model started speaking live.

A token every twenty seconds, day after day, at a cursor where the future does not exist and nothing can be replayed. The experiment became a promise — and a promise is made to someone. For the first time we saw the second reader clearly, and we saw what he could not see: our weeks, our judges, our untouched reserves were, to him, words. A record is only evidence to the people who watched it being made. To everyone else it is a memory, and memories are ours to edit.

We asked ourselves the honest question — how would a stranger know? — and gave ourselves the honest answer: he wouldn't. Not until he can check without us.

That answer started a second body of work we had not planned when we started the first.

What we built, layer by layer

The idea began simply: put every decision in an envelope, seal it, open it later. Each layer after that was the answer to a specific way the previous layer could still lie.

Every token, including silence. An envelope proves what is inside it; it does not say how many envelopes there were, or whether an inconvenient one got lost. So we commit every twenty-second token of the tape — 4,320 a day — whether the model calls or stays silent. Silence is sealed too. The fingerprint names exactly two things: the moment and the claim (long, short, or nothing), each mixed with 32 bytes of fresh randomness so that a three-way answer cannot be guessed from its hash.

One chain. Each fingerprint depends on the one before it. Remove a token, insert one, swap a week for another week — and every hash after the cut stops matching what has already left the building.

Someone else's clock. Our own seal is worth nothing: we could write any date on it. So every five minutes the fingerprints of that interval close into a Merkle root that is signed and sent to clocks we do not control — an RFC 3161 timestamp and an entry in Sigstore's public transparency log, typically within twenty seconds of the interval closing. Every hour the root is anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain through OpenTimestamps, whose block time no one can rewrite. Each call additionally receives its own RFC 3161 stamp at birth, published with the call. From that second on, we are as unable to change the past as anyone else.

A sealed count. Alongside each five-minute root travels a salted commitment to how many calls that interval contained. Not which — how many. It is opened later with everything else, so the number of calls in any window is fixed before the window's outcome exists.

Delayed reveal, full disclosure. A call is revealed only after the market has answered it and never earlier than a day after birth — late enough that it cannot help anyone trade, early enough that it can help everyone check. Ninety-six hours after the UTC day ends, everything is opened: every token, every salt, the pack for the whole day. Anyone can recompute the roots from the first envelope to the last and compare them with what the outside clocks saw in real time.

What the envelope contains — and only that. The moment and the claim. A stranger can verify what we said and when, down to the second. The record proves the stream, not the mind behind it; that is what a record is for.

One key, one genesis, one chain, continuous since 30 August 2026. That is the whole machine. It runs by itself; no one touches it.

Inviting the skeptics

Then we did the thing that had served us best for eighteen months: we sat the skeptics at our table and let them attack. Not one — a whole gallery of them, each with a different accusation. Every time one of them found a crack, we did not patch the crack. We wrote a rule and put it into the code and into the public specification, where the next reader can hold us to it.

The painter says the history was drawn afterwards. External clocks answer him: the fingerprint of a call exists in a log we do not run before the market has moved. To paint, one would have to rewrite Rekor and Bitcoin.

The editor says we deleted the misses. Every token is sealed, including silence, and every five-minute interval contains exactly as many leaves as it has twenty-second slots — fifteen, not fourteen. The count of calls is committed before the outcome. There is nowhere to hide a deletion.

The splicer says we stitched the best stretches from several runs into one. The chain forbids it: a stretch from another run carries another predecessor hash and other witnesses, and the roots of that interval — already timestamped by someone else — would not match. A record like ours can be continued but not assembled.

The clairvoyant says the model saw the future. The live stack physically cannot: it receives only events that have already arrived and been finalized, and it commits its claim before the answer exists. We turned this into a rule the reader can test on every call — the external timestamp of a call must precede the moment the market resolved it — and measured the margin. Across the first days of live calls the closest a resolution ever came to its stamp was 4,565 seconds, about seventy-six minutes; the fastest resolution anywhere in the sixty-three-week history took 120 seconds, while a live call is committed within about twenty. A violation would mark the call invalid and count it as a miss. There are none.

The picker is the most serious of them, and the one we spent the longest with. He does not accuse us of forgery. He says: you could have run ten of these in parallel, sealed each honestly, and shown me the one that won. He is right that a seal cannot refute him — a seal proves what a record is, not that it was the only one. Two things answer him, and neither is cryptographic.

The first is arithmetic. Selecting the best of N honest runs buys about √(2 ln N) standard deviations of luck: two for ten runs, under four for a thousand, five for a million. Measured on folded thoughts rather than raw calls, so that echoes cannot inflate the count, the record stood 8.5 standard deviations from chance at launch. That figure treats neighbouring thoughts as independent, which they are not entirely, so we read it as a yardstick rather than a p-value; at the harshest fold we tried, a full hour, it falls to 3.2 (note 20). Selection cannot manufacture a record that keeps holding after its rules are frozen — which is why the weeks after the freeze matter more than any number here. Selection is a mortal threat to short records and nearly powerless against long, dense ones — provided the record is shown whole, which is precisely what the four-day pack enforces.

The second is a date. What can be done against the picker is to name the official record before its results exist. So we did: a signed manifest that binds one public key, one genesis, one chain, and declares that any conflicting root under that key disqualifies the whole record. Its boundary is 3 September 2026, 00:00 UTC. The days before it — the first live days — are kept exactly as they were sealed and labelled for what they are: a prelaunch record. The days after it are the official one. We would rather draw that line honestly at day four than pretend it was never needed.

The archivist says that one day a salt will go missing and an inconvenient token will simply fail to open. So the rule is written in advance: an unrevealed token counts as a miss, is marked as such in the pack, and cannot be quietly dropped; a late reveal may show its contents but never improves the fixed statistic; a missing pack is that many misses and a record on hold. Losing salts is now the most expensive thing we could do.

The skeptic says all of this is a record of decisions, not a record of results. He is right, and we say so on the page. What the seals prove is that a stream of decisions was fixed before the market answered and was never edited.

Where proof ends

Here is the boundary, stated plainly, because we respect whoever is reading.

A seal proves what was: this sequence of decisions was born in time, in full, and was not touched after the market spoke. A seal cannot prove what was not — that there were no other sequences, no other rooms, no other keys. Nobody can prove that: not an audited institution, not a published laboratory, not us. Every attempt to prove a negative fact opens another room behind the last one; the regress is infinite, and at some point it stops being science and becomes a mood.

What can be done instead is three things, and we have done them. Declare early, so that the choice of the official record is dated before its results. Disclose everything, so that the record is shown whole and the arithmetic of selection has nothing to work with. And then let volume and time do what no signature can: every week that arrives from here is a week that could not have been chosen in hindsight.

We are equally plain about what the seals do not claim. They do not claim the model is good; only the tape can grade that, and it does so one call at a time. They claim one thing, and they claim it completely: each decision, whatever produced it, was fixed before its outcome — the record does not need our word.

Living the record

Formally the live record began on 30 August 2026, with the first sealed token. In our own experience it began the day we saw the boundary above and stopped arguing with it. Before that we were defending the record. After it, we simply live it.

The first two speaking days are already on the tape, side by side, forever: one bad — 334 calls, 43% of them right — and one very good — 491 calls, nine in ten right so far — with no way to keep one and lose the other. The reader is renewed each week; each renewal takes effect only forward, never on a call already born, and the handover itself is sealed like everything else. Research continues beside the record, because we cannot help it — we still want to know why the model falls silent for hours and then speaks in bursts, what it does in weather it has never seen, whether its best moments have a shape. None of it touches the stream. The past belongs to whoever is reading.

We share this not because we are certain. We do not know what comes next; that is the point. One thing we do know: whatever it is, we will not be able to rewrite it. That is what we wanted to give you — not a result, but a way of keeping results that does not need anyone's word, including ours.

How to check

Everything the checking requires is public: the key, the genesis, the five-minute witnesses with their transparency-log entries, the hourly OpenTimestamps receipts, the daily packs, and a verifier that recomputes the chain from the first envelope to the last. The instructions that follow are written three times — for a reader without a terminal, for a reader with one, and as a single prompt you can hand to your own assistant. Any of the three takes a few minutes.

If you have no time to check, watch forward: next week will prove more than any sentence here. If you are the kind who waits, wait. The stack grows on its own, twenty seconds at a time.

Method notes: the machine described here is the public Proof Tape under /proof — key, genesis, five-minute witnesses with transparency-log entries, hourly OpenTimestamps receipts, the canonical track manifest and the stand-alone verifier. Figures quoted (margins, counts) are those of the first live days and are dated in the text; the verifier recomputes everything from the public tree and needs nothing from us.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 25 · AXIOM 5.1

From committee to cadence: what AXIOM 5.1 kept, and what it gave up

TWO GENERATIONS ON ONE PAGE · WHAT CARRIED OVER · WHAT WAS RETIRED, AND WHY · NO ARCHIVE FIGURE REGRADED

A reader who works through the archive below will meet a different machine from the one on the dashboard: a committee of seventy snapshots, a conviction gate at 0.90, an asymmetric simulator, costs charged per side, fifty-six weeks. Then the page above speaks of one reader reborn every week, a symmetric ±1% exam, sixty-three weeks. Both are true; they are two generations of the same laboratory. This note is the bridge, because a journal that lets its reader infer the transition from clues is not append-only — it is merely unedited.

What carried over, unchanged

The token language (note 07) — the market read as event-time microstructure, not candles — and its lookahead law: not a single bit from the future, enforced by gated pipelines that refuse to publish a lineage they cannot verify. The judge as a separate, continuous price record that we never mark ourselves, and the willingness to lose three perfect weeks to it (note 02). Walk-forward weeks with an untouched reserve beyond every training cutoff. The law that windows are not trades (note 11), which the present record applies as the fold: thirty-two thousand calls are counted as 1,134 thoughts, and the fold is attacked until it stops moving (note 20). And the two lessons that shaped how this page argues at all — that selection can wear any fingerprint (notes 14, 18), so no showcase is offered here as proof, only the exam that accumulates forward.

What was retired

The committee. The ensemble of seventy was many ages of one mind voting on the present (note 13). It worked, and the frozen-copy autopsy (note 19) explained why it had to change: a fixed set of weights, however well chosen, begins dying the day it leaves the tape — and a committee is a fixed set of weights with a longer half-life, not an escape from the law. The insight the committee carried — that time is the diversity that matters — survives in a simpler form: one reader, reborn each week, examined once on a week beyond its training, retired. What persists is the process, not any one file of weights.

The gates and the simulators. The archive’s figures were earned under a conviction gate, an asymmetric frame and a cost model that belonged to that era’s exam. The present track answers to one frame only — symmetric ±1% first-touch, graded on trade prints — and one speaking rule, frozen in public on 30 August 2026 and applied identically to every week, earlier and later alike. Fewer knobs; every remaining knob published.

Checkpoint governance. Note 05 drew a rule from an old run — never let one curve pick your model — and the committee era answered it by treating checkpoints as a population and promoting by stability. AXIOM 5.1 takes the rule to its end: no selection at all. Each week’s reader is the final step of its training, with no best-of-anything; a control run proved that choice neutral to the last tensor. There is no curve to pick from, so no curve can flatter us.

What the change costs

A committee smooths; a single reader does not. Its bad week is on the record at full weight, next to its good one, with nothing to average it away — you can see both on the first days of the live track. We consider that a price worth paying for a machine whose every part is inspectable and whose only defence is the exam.

Method notes: no archive figure has been regraded or restated; each archive note carries the frame it was written under. The neutrality of that choice was verified on the same sealed cache along a deterministic path: every tensor identical after the control run.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 24 · AXIOM 5.1

Standing on measured ground: the microstructure our tokens speak

A VOCABULARY WITH FORTY YEARS OF LITERATURE BEHIND IT · EVERY FAMILY SEATED BY ABLATION · THE CONTROL MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED

A common way to build a “quant” model is to invent exotic indicators and name them after yourself. We went the other way. Almost every family in our token vocabulary is a quantity that market-microstructure research spent decades defining, measuring and arguing about — not because borrowed authority is comfortable, but because each one is a hypothesis about mechanics that survived peer review and replication. And in this lab no family keeps its seat on reputation: the test is always the same — remove it, retrain the reader, and watch what the record loses. Ablation is the only argument we accept from a feature.

What the families assert — and how each one lives here. Signed flow and its imbalance: trades are not symmetric events; who initiated matters [1], and imbalance in that directional force is among the most robust short-horizon predictors the literature knows [2]. The perpetual tape we read prints the aggressor natively — what Lee and Ready built a classifier to infer is, on our venue, a fact of the record — and that force, bar by bar, is the first thing our reader breathes. Price impact per unit of flow: Kyle’s λ [3] says a market has a measurable stiffness — how far price yields per unit of net flow — and that the stiffness itself changes character; our reader watches it change on a 20-second clock, where regime turns arrive first. The price of liquidity: Amihud’s ratio [4] prices movement per dollar of turnover; when that price spikes, the market has thinned — and a reader that watches turnover on a 20-second clock feels the thinning before it becomes a move. Event time: information arrives in bursts, not calendar ticks [5]. We hold a strict 20-second cadence so the record stays auditable — and let the burst structure be measured inside the window rather than assumed away. The book and the tape: the families are public ground; the composition — which of them this generation of the reader hears, in what proportion, across which horizons — is where the lab’s own work lives. What we publish is the test every family had to pass to hold its seat, and the record above, which is that composition being measured.

We have also run the control, on ourselves. The same class of reader, fed a classical price-indicator diet instead of measured microstructure, earned an order of magnitude less per speaking window — the baseline duel of note 12, replayed at the level of inputs instead of strategies, with the same verdict. None of these families is our invention, and that is the point: each is measured ground, a quantity whose meaning does not depend on our say-so. What is ours is the composition — how the families interact, nonlinearly, across horizons, inside one sequence model. The signal, wherever it lives, lives there; that interaction surface is exactly what a deep model can represent and a fixed formula cannot. The record on this page is the composition being measured.

Method notes: every family above is computed strictly causally — the lookahead law of note 07 applies to each. Families are named at the level the literature names them; the composition is argued the only way that counts here — by the out-of-sample record above.

REFERENCES
  1. Lee, C., Ready, M. “Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data.” Journal of Finance, 1991.
  2. Cont, R., Kukanov, A., Stoikov, S. “The Price Impact of Order Book Events.” Journal of Financial Econometrics, 2014.
  3. Kyle, A. “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading.” Econometrica, 1985.
  4. Amihud, Y. “Illiquidity and Stock Returns.” Journal of Financial Markets, 2002.
  5. Easley, D., López de Prado, M., O’Hara, M. “The Volume Clock.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2012.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 23 · PREVIOUS TRACK

Frozen quotes: the anatomy of a dead bar

578 STILL STRETCHES FOUND · 376 CALLS RULED INELIGIBLE · THE RULE PREDATES THE AUDIT · BOTH NUMBERS PUBLISHED

FILED ON THE PREVIOUS TRACK · 25 AUG 2026The present track is judged on trade prints, where a frozen quote cannot impersonate a market. The rule below remains this lab’s hygiene law for any quote-fed instrument; its figures belong to the previous track and are preserved exactly as filed.

Zoom deep enough into any long tape and you will find stretches where the quote simply stops moving — thin nights, feed hiccups, a market holding its breath. Our record contains 578 such stretches of five minutes or longer (the longest: over four hours in a September night). The bars are all there — the tape has zero gaps — but a frozen quote is a dead instrument: features computed on it describe nothing, and a model reading them is reading a photograph, not a market.

This lab’s operating law has said so for a long time: a bar whose quote has not updated is not tradeable. When we audited what that rule actually touches, the verdict was one-sided: 592 calls of the old ledger’s 39,452 (1.5%) were born inside still stretches — and they resolved at barely a third correct (35.8%), far below anything else the model does. Phantom signals on phantom features, graded mostly as misses. Two ways to apply the rule, both published: strike the dead calls and nothing else, and the ledger reads 64.3% on 38,860; apply eligibility at the source, the way the live pipeline does — a dead bar never enters the record at all, and the next live calls in strict chronological order take the places the dead ones had been occupying — and the ledger settles at 39,076 calls, 64.5%. We use the second, because it is exactly what the live gate produces. Neither is a repaint: no call is moved, recoloured or re-judged, no call is chosen by its outcome — one blind rule keys on the state of the quote at the moment of birth, and the queue advances the way time itself would have advanced it.

We would have applied the rule identically had the group been all hits — that is what makes it data hygiene rather than curation. Both readings stay published, side by side: 63.9 raw, 64.5 eligible. Six tenths of a point — disclosed, not discovered by a skeptic.

One asymmetry is worth naming: the first bar after a stretch wakes — the quote has updated, the bar is live, and calls born there stay on the record. Only the photographs are excluded; the first real frame is not.

Method notes: a still stretch is ≥15 consecutive 20-second bars with identical high and low of the perpetual mid-quote; eligibility keys on bar state at call time (fully causal — the live gate uses quote age, known at decision time). The pre-rule ledger, the rule, and the audit that measured it are all archived; every figure of that track read from the eligible ledger.

REFERENCES
  1. Sambasivan, N. et al. “‘Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work’: Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI.” CHI, 2021.
  2. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 21 · AXIOM 5.1

The record, day by day: 437 days, nothing edited

EVERY DAY OF THE TRACK · 243 SPEAKING · 194 SILENT · DRAWN FROM THE PUBLISHED LEDGER AS FILED

Aggregates can hide almost anything, so here is the opposite of an aggregate: the entire record, one cell per day, nothing chosen and nothing left out. Green is a day the model finished right more often than wrong; earth-red is a day it finished wrong; an empty outline is a day it declined to speak at all. Hover any cell — each carries its own numbers.

The same record, folded into months

Fold the days into calendar months and the texture becomes a shape. Fourteen of fifteen months clear the 55% break-even; the record’s worst month — November 2025, 53.8% across 2,782 calls — stands here at full height, because a record that cannot show its worst month cannot be trusted with its best. The system walked out of that month into a December at 77.3%, which is the pattern this whole site keeps repeating: the failures are coherent, bounded, and survivable, and the recovery is part of the record, not a promise.

Method notes: daily and monthly cells aggregate the published ledger as filed (trade-print judge, tick-resolved), not the versioned entry-aware benchmark now on the dashboard; a “day” is a UTC day. Cell colours quantize hit-rate only; call counts are in each cell’s hover passport.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 22 · AXIOM 5.1

The geometry of patience: what each horizon is allowed to look like

ROLLING WINDOWS, EVERY START DATE · ONE WEEK TO ONE YEAR · THE ENVELOPE NARROWS ABOVE THE BAR

The most common way to be fooled by a track record — in both directions — is to read it at the wrong horizon. So we measured, on our own record, exactly how much any horizon is allowed to tremble: every possible window of each length, its full historical range, its middle 80%, its median. The result is a funnel — and the funnel is the honest shape of this system.

Weeks are weather; half-years are climate

Read the funnel left to right. A week is allowed to look like anything: the record contains weeks at 0.8% and weeks at 100%, and a third of all weeks finish below the bar — with streaks of three in a row on file. A month still swings from 41 to 97. No quarter has finished below break-even on this record — its lowest window stands at 56.1%, in the cold season. But from six months up, the trembling stops: no half-year window in this record has ever finished below break-even; the tightest band, the year, stayed inside 67–70.

This is what predictive skill actually looks like from inside — not a steady drip of wins but a wide, violent distribution whose center refuses to move. The practical reading for a skeptic: judge this system at the horizon we claim, and hold us to it. If any six-month stretch of the growing public record ever finishes below its bar, that is not weather — that is the system failing at its own stated resolution, and it will be visible here the day it happens.

Method notes: windows are rolling with every start week; figures are call-weighted over the same published ledger. The bands quoted are historical description, not a guarantee of the future — the point of publishing the envelope is precisely that a breach of it cannot be renegotiated after the fact.

REFERENCES
  1. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
  2. Lo, A. “The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2004.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 19 · AXIOM 5.1

The frozen-copy autopsy: we froze our own reader and watched it die

ONE SNAPSHOT, FROZEN · 60 UNSEEN WEEKS REPLAYED BLIND · BIT-EXACT HARNESS VERIFIED · THE CADENCE WALKED THE SAME TAPE

Every claim about non-stationarity is secretly a claim about your own system, so we ran the experiment nobody enjoys: we took one of our own readers — the very first of the walk-forward line — froze its weights and its normalization exactly as they stood, and replayed it blind across all sixty weeks that followed. No retraining, no adjustment, no mercy. The same weeks, the same judge, the same symmetric ±1% exam that grades the living system.

First, the control that makes the experiment mean anything: replayed on the one week it was born for, the frozen copy reproduced its original grading file bit for bit — byte-identical output on a fresh machine. Whatever follows is the market drifting away from a mind, not a harness drifting away from itself.

Then the sixty weeks. The copy did not die politely. It coasted for a season on what it remembered — a first quarter close behind the living system. It spent a cold stretch level with it, because in that stretch there was little for either to know. Then the market moved on, and the snapshot did something more interesting than fading: it inverted. In its ninth-to-twelfth month it scored deep below chance — confidently, coherently wrong — while the weekly cadence, walking the same tape with the same architecture and the same exam, stayed above its break-even. By the end of the replay the frozen copy’s ledger summed to approximately zero: fourteen months of calls, nothing earned, the last third actively toxic.

Drift is not decay — it is inversion

The textbook picture of concept drift is a slow fade toward the coin [1]. What the autopsy shows is sharper and stranger: the geometry the snapshot had memorized did not stop existing — it started resolving the other way, and the snapshot’s conviction machinery, still perfectly calibrated to a vanished world, concentrated its largest bets exactly where that world had moved on. The strictest conviction bands died first and hardest. Confidence, in a frozen mind, curdles into anti-knowledge. This rhymes with what our own inversion note recorded from the outside a generation ago; the autopsy shows the mechanism from the inside.

What this buys the record

Three things, and we consider them among the most load-bearing facts on this site. First, the weekly cadence is not an engineering preference — it is the measured difference between a living system and a dead one: same architecture, same features, same exam, one variable changed. Second, drift is now a number in our archive rather than a fear: it is visible within a quarter and fatal within a year, which calibrates exactly how much staleness the discipline may ever tolerate. Third — no single file of weights is the result: a snapshot begins dying the day it leaves the cadence, and its own confidence is the poison. What persists is the process that keeps producing readers.

Method notes: the frozen copy and the living line share the architecture, feature language, judge and exam; the sole variable is retraining. The bit-exact control was verified on an independently provisioned machine before the replay was trusted. Quarterly figures aggregate the same per-call ledger the dashboard was built from when this note was filed; per-week frozen-vs-living tapes are archived in full.

REFERENCES
  1. Gama, J. et al. “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation.” ACM Computing Surveys, 2014.
  2. Lo, A. “The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2004.
  3. Hendrycks, D. et al. “The Many Faces of Robustness.” ICCV, 2021.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 20 · AXIOM 5.1

The fold that would not break: counting thoughts instead of ticks

32,083 CALLS · FOLDED INTO 1,134 EPISODES · FOLD THRESHOLD SWEPT 40s → 1 HOUR · SIGNIFICANCE SURVIVES THE ENTIRE SWEEP

CORRECTION · NOVEMBER 2026The σ figures in this note treat neighbouring episodes as independent binomial trials. They are not entirely independent, so the figures overstate certainty: read them as a yardstick of how far the record sits from a coin, not as significance levels. The site’s position is in the questions for skeptics. Every figure below is kept as filed.

The oldest sin of signal research is counting the same insight twice. A confident model does not speak once — it speaks in bursts: one good read of the tape, echoed for minutes. Grade the echoes as independent evidence and any t-statistic will flatter you; the literature has warned about exactly this arithmetic for decades [1][2]. A generation ago this lab wrote “windows are not trades” on its wall. This note is that law, rebuilt for the present record — and then attacked until it refused to break.

The fold rule is deliberately primitive: consecutive calls separated by less than about a hundred seconds of silence belong to one episode — one thought, one verdict, majority-graded. Under it, the 32,083 published calls collapse to 1,134 episodes, and it is on episodes, not calls, that this site quotes significance: 62.6% of thoughts resolve in the model’s favour, 8.5σ from chance. The reduction is a factor of twenty-eight, applied by us, to our own headline — because the honest unit of evidence is the thought, not the tick.

Attacking the fold

Any single threshold invites the obvious objection: you chose it. So we swept it. Fold at 40 seconds and the record holds 1,668 thoughts at 11.0σ. Fold at five minutes: 6.1σ. Fifteen minutes: 4.3σ. Half an hour: 3.7σ. Fold at a full hour — collapsing everything the model says inside any sixty-minute window into a single verdict, a reduction no honest critic would demand — and 328 thoughts remain, still 3.2σ from chance. The conclusion does not depend on the knife.

Why neighbouring thoughts are not one thought

Two structural facts protect the count. Each episode is judged from its own entry price by first-touch — neighbouring episodes are graded on different journeys of the tape, not one journey re-counted; and episodes are near-unanimous inside (99% resolve cleanly one way), which is what you expect of a thought and not of a smear. The deeper point belongs to the exam itself: a symmetric ±1% race from a moving entry is a different question every time it is asked. The market answers each one separately; we merely refuse to count the model’s repetitions of its own answer.

Method notes: fold thresholds applied to the identical published ledger (same judge, same healed verdicts of the two repaired weeks, same tick-resolved tail); σ figures are binomial tests of episode-majority correctness against one half. Episode boundaries and per-episode verdicts ship inside the dashboard’s own data — the fold is inspectable in the page source.

REFERENCES
  1. Newey, W., West, K. “A Simple, Positive Semi-definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix.” Econometrica, 1987.
  2. White, H. “A Reality Check for Data Snooping.” Econometrica, 2000.
  3. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 17

The isolated autopsy: we aimed a second research line at our own model

ISOLATED RED-TEAM LINE · A SEPARATE CLAUDE AGENT · FULL DATA ACCESS · PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES · SEALED HOLDOUTS · NO SIGHT OF OUR RESULTS

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Mid-expedition, we commissioned the harshest audit we could design: a second research line, isolated from the first — a separate Claude agent in its own environment, with its own tooling and zero shared code with the main effort — was given our raw Bitcoin corpus, freedom to source anything public it wanted, and one adversarial brief: find whatever simple, linear, classical structure we might have missed. It was shown none of our results. If simple structure existed, it had every chance to embarrass us.

It worked the way we would want to be prosecuted: hypotheses pre-registered before testing, a trial ledger with significance thresholds that rise with every attempt, sealed holdout zones, Newey–West corrections for overlapping windows, equal-weighted days, costs charged on position turnover. Across the families it closed — time-of-day, funding quadrants, positioning, flow exhaustion, volatility compression, basis, liquidation cascades, absorption, cross-sectional oversold baskets, calendar structure — the verdict was consistent and beautiful: six microstructure mechanisms are real (pre-registered sign confirmed, |t| 2.6–5.6), and every one of them is two to five times too small to survive the cost of acting on it.

Three times, from three different causes, the audit rediscovered a law this lab had carved into its own wall: event statistics flatter; only a one-position simulator on untouched data tells the truth. An oversold basket printed t-statistics above 4 on all sixteen instruments — and lost 39% on walk-forward, because sixteen correlated cryptos are one observation wearing sixteen costumes. Two research lines, zero shared code, one conclusion: windows are not trades.

The autopsy’s capstone measured the ocean itself. Bitcoin’s median realized volatility has halved — from 78% in 2021 to roughly 40% today; it has not touched 140% annualized even once since 2022. Every classical, capitulation-class effect it confirmed needs breathing room that Bitcoin no longer offers — on the audit’s own gate, the flagship classical candidate finds one qualifying trade in five and a half years of BTC. In liquid altcoins, still breathing at 88–101%, the same class of structure remains alive and priced — one of the candidates our expansion pipeline is built to measure properly.

What we take from being prosecuted and acquitted: in the asset we chose, simple structure no longer covers its own costs — which is precisely why a nonlinear reader of raw flow was worth building, and why whatever it finds is not in a textbook. The full audit trail — pre-registrations, closed families, the corrections that killed each mirage — stays in our archive, and its discipline has been folded into how this lab prosecutes itself.

Postscript. Days after this note was filed, the prosecution escalated: we armed a counterfeiter with full look-ahead and our own selection machinery, and let two isolated research lines run nearly two hundred forged committees against this record. What they managed to imitate — and the one thing none of them could — is note 18.

Method notes: the red-team line kept its own environment and trial journal; the summary here compresses its written findings. Its one surviving alt-market candidate is described in outline only while it matures in our expansion queue.

REFERENCES
  1. Newey, W., West, K. “A Simple, Positive Semi-definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix.” Econometrica, 1987.
  2. Harvey, C., Liu, Y. “Evaluating Trading Strategies.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2014.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 18

The forgery test: we built a counterfeiter and gave it every advantage

~190 FORGED COMMITTEES · TWO ISOLATED RESEARCH LINES · FULL LOOK-AHEAD GRANTED · ZERO FULL PROFILES REPRODUCED

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

The sharpest attack we could imagine on this record is not a critic — it is a counterfeiter. So we built one, and armed it beyond fairness: thousands of technical-analysis rules crossed with regime filters and randomized composition; committees assembled by greedy optimization aimed directly at the final return curve; full sight of the entire history — the one advantage no honest system ever gets; and, in the harshest series, our own selection machinery, handed over to noise. Two isolated research lines ran the campaign — separate code, separate candidate pools, one shared judge and cost model. Nearly two hundred forged committees, in six waves.

The forgeries were good. Disturbingly good. On the stretch they were allowed to see, they painted win-rate curves to within a few points of ours; they passed the even-eighths consistency test; they were invariant to entry phase; a share of them wore behavioural fingerprints resembling our members’; armed with our own optimizer, they even reproduced the membership-overlap statistics we once treated as a defence. Five of the six defences we had built for this record turned out to be forgeable. We publish that map deliberately: knowing which metrics noise can wear is worth more than pretending it cannot — and it is why none of those five is presented as evidence anywhere on this site.

One thing no forgery managed. Marched beyond the data it was selected on, every family of counterfeits died — every wave, both lines: median forward return −11.5 bps per call, and the single best configuration of the entire campaign reached +10.5. The genuine selection, run once per split with no retries, landed at +17 to +20 bps per call on unseen stretches, at 74–75% win-rates, invariant to which call starts the sequence — and the whole ladder of splits, from the harshest quarter-selection up, points the same way. On the ladder where the complete profile was scored, the count was exact: zero of fifty-seven. On the one axis that cannot be painted — return on data the selection had not seen — the gap between the record and its best forgery did not close.

The lesson is carved into how this page argues. A showcase — any showcase, ours included — can be manufactured by selection alone, so no showcase is offered here as proof. What we offer is the thing the campaign could not fake: transfer. The blind march of note 14, the sequenced simulators of note 11, and the live tape accumulating ahead of this sentence — where forgery is dead by construction, because no one has seen the data yet.

Method notes: same sequenced judge throughout (±1% symmetric and 3:1 frame, 24h clock, costs 10 bps per side); candidate pools frozen before selection in every arm; the counterfeiter was granted look-ahead and unlimited retries, the genuine side ran once per split; figures are campaign-wide medians and maxima, not curated examples. The full trial ledger stays in the archive.

REFERENCES
