  2. Sullivan, R., Timmermann, A., White, H. “Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap.” Journal of Finance, 1999.
  3. Bailey, D., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., Zhu, Q. “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting.” Journal of Computational Finance, 2017.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 11

Windows are not trades: what a one-position simulator does to beautiful statistics

GREEDY REPLAY · ONE POSITION AT A TIME · COSTS DEDUCTED · ENTRY-PHASE INVARIANCE TESTED

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

Every signal researcher eventually meets the same siren: a model that fires thousands of confident calls, most of them correct. The number is real — and it can still be worth nothing. Confident calls arrive in clusters: one good moment, echoed for minutes on end. Counted as windows, one insight masquerades as a hundred victories; counted as actions, only the first of them could ever be acted on, because by then the rest are describing a decision already taken.

So the lab grades its ensemble the only way a simulator would experience it: a greedy, strictly chronological replay. First signal takes the position; every signal that arrives while the position lives is ignored; the exit — target, stop, or clock — frees the simulator for the next first signal. No look-ahead, no choosing among a cluster after the fact: the replay needs exactly one bit of state, am I in a trade or not.

Under that discipline, roughly 2,900 consensus windows on the public track collapse into between 117 and 147 independent trades, depending only on the exit clock. Those trades — not the windows — are the statistic we quote: in the patient profile, nearly nine trades in ten close positive after costs. One number that must always travel with that one: the patient frame is asymmetric — objective +1%, adverse bound −3% — so 77.5% is merely break-even there; a win-rate is only as good as its margin above that bar. The margin is what we watch, and the symmetric strict ±1% exam is published right next to it. The return-weighted t-statistics sit far beyond conventional significance even after multiple-testing corrections. The same audit, run on our loudest single checkpoint — sixty-two thousand windows of apparent brilliance — collapsed it to a coin flip. We killed that candidate ourselves, before it ever left the lab.

One more invariance matters to anyone reading this record: where you start. A simulator that begins at the first signal, or the third, or the tenth, converges to the same sequence after its first exit — measured across ten starting phases, the hit-rate moves by less than half a percentage point. The record you see is not one lucky path through the cluster; it is the only path, up to a few boundary trades.

Method notes: entries at the consensus bar close; exits by first touch of a fixed bracket, by its mirror stop, or by clock; costs deducted per side. Trade-level t-statistics treat trades as independent; dependence through shared regimes is addressed by segment-wise consistency (eight consecutive segments, seven positive, one flat) rather than assumed away.

REFERENCES
  1. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
  2. Harvey, C., Liu, Y. “Backtesting.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2015.
  3. White, H. “A Reality Check for Data Snooping.” Econometrica, 2000.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 12

Twenty textbook strategies, one table: the baseline duel

MA CROSSES · RSI · BOLLINGER · PARAMETERS TUNED IN THEIR FAVOUR · IDENTICAL SIMULATOR, BRACKETS, COSTS

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Any track record owes its reader one uncomfortable experiment: could a textbook have done this? We seated twenty classical strategies at exactly our table — moving-average crosses across a grid of windows, RSI bands, Bollinger reversions and breakouts — and, to be maximally unfair to ourselves, let each one tune its parameters on the full history it was judged on. Same one-position simulator, same brackets, same costs, same price record.

The best of the twenty finished at +220 basis points over the whole period — a 0.9-sigma result, statistically indistinguishable from flipping coins after fees. Most finished below zero. The ensemble, on identical rules, earned more than an order of magnitude more, at a significance level that survives every correction we know how to apply. The gap is the measurable distance between filtering a price line and reading the flow that produces it.

The result is consistent with three decades of literature: simple technical rules showed promise on mid-century data [1], and then data-snooping-aware re-examinations watched that promise evaporate on modern, cost-honest tape [2]. Our contribution is only rigour of setting: same simulator, same era, same costs, adversarially tuned baselines — and a specialist model on the other side of the table.

Why the gap exists is the more interesting question. An indicator is a fixed linear functional of recent prices — a moving average is a dot product, an RSI a ratio of two of them. The information that decides the next hundred basis points lives deeper: in how aggression clusters, how the book leans before it breaks, which silences precede which moves — relations that are conditional, compositional, and nonlinear. A deep sequence model can represent those; a dot product cannot. The duel does not prove our model is clever. It is evidence that the signal, wherever it lives, is not linearly extractable from price — which may be precisely why it is still there.

Method notes: baseline families and parameter grids fixed in advance; per-family best reported (a favourable treatment — their numbers are upper bounds). All runs share the graded price record and cost model of the public track.

REFERENCES
  1. Brock, W., Lakonishok, J., LeBaron, B. “Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns.” Journal of Finance, 1992.
  2. Sullivan, R., Timmermann, A., White, H. “Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap.” Journal of Finance, 1999.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 13

A mixture of seventy: why the orchestra outplays every soloist

1,700+ CANDIDATES · 1,119 SOLOISTS AUDITED · NONE SURVIVED ALONE · THE MIXTURE DID

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

Here is the finding we did not expect to be so absolute. We took over 1,700 candidate checkpoints from three training populations and audited every one with enough signal volume as a standalone strategy — the full one-position simulator, costs included. Not one survived. The best soloist in seventeen hundred reached about a sigma and a half: the territory of luck. The mixture of seventy, drawn from that same pool, clears discovery-grade significance. The skill does not live in any single network. It lives between them.

The mechanism is visible in the audit. A training run is one entity moving along a trajectory: every hundred steps we photograph it, and each photograph is the same mind at a different age — naive early, specialized in the middle, loud and self-certain late. Each age is fluent in a narrow slice of market weather: the median expert contributes meaningfully in only a handful of weeks. The ensemble is not an average of opinions; it is a relay of specialists — in most trades on the record, the deciding voice belongs to a different small subset of experts than the trade before. Consensus is the baton pass.

We tested the fashionable alternative, because it is beautiful and cheap: average the weights of the champions into a single network — model soups, stochastic weight averaging [2][3]. The soup is calm, smooth — and mediocre: averaging in weight space cancels exactly the disagreements that carry the information. Selective consensus keeps the specialists intact and lets the market decide, moment by moment, whose regime is on. Mixtures of experts have been rediscovered every decade since 1991 [1]; markets, with their rotating regimes, may be one of the domains that suit them best.

None of this is a private heresy. The most storied quantitative houses of the last three decades — the Renaissances and D.E. Shaws of the world — are, by every account that has escaped them, not one grand idea but disciplined ensembles of many modest, decorrelated edges, voted and re-voted in production [4]. We admire that lineage, and we make no comparison of scale — only of philosophy. Our contribution runs on a different axis: an ensemble drawn not from many ideas, but from many ages of one mind.

Two engineering details matter. Each expert speaks only when its conviction clears a demanding bar, and the later, louder ages of the entity are held to stricter standards of conviction than the quiet middle — a discipline set by temperament, not by outcome. And composition is audited by ablation — the standard robustness rite: remove any single expert and replay the simulator. No member’s absence moves the result by more than single-digit percent; two systematic contrarians surfaced by the audit were removed before the live stretch began, and the live data then delivered its own verdict on them, unprompted — one stayed silent, the other fired twelve times and missed twelve times.

Method notes: soloist audits and the ensemble share one replay engine, one cost model, one graded record. Expert identities are anonymized in these notes; the replay methodology itself is described in full, because the method is the part worth checking.

REFERENCES
  1. Jacobs, R., Jordan, M., Nowlan, S., Hinton, G. “Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts.” Neural Computation, 1991.
  2. Wortsman, M. et al. “Model Soups: Averaging Weights of Multiple Fine-Tuned Models.” ICML, 2022.
  3. Izmailov, P. et al. “Averaging Weights Leads to Wider Optima and Better Generalization.” UAI, 2018.
  4. Zuckerman, G. The Man Who Solved the Market. Portfolio, 2019.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 14

The selection alibi: the ensemble was recognizable before its results existed

BLIND RE-SELECTION ON THE EARLIEST QUARTER · POSITIVE ACROSS THE UNSEEN REMAINDER · WIN-RATE 4σ ABOVE COIN FLIP

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

The sharpest question a quant can ask about any committee is quiet and lethal: did you just pick the winners after watching them win? Selection bias does not need bad faith — it only needs enough candidates and a long enough record. So we prosecuted our own selection, and this note is the alibi.

Members of the ensemble do carry a measurable temperament, visible long before their results accumulate: they are an order of magnitude more selective than the candidate pool (speaking rarely, on an even rhythm, without manic bursts), and their scarce early calls land better. On the earliest quarter of the public record alone, these traits identify future members against the pool with AUC up to 0.94. We report this as a portrait, not as proof: when we later built forged committees from pure noise, a share of them wore similar signatures — behavioural fingerprints of this kind can be imitated [see note 18]. What follows cannot.

Then the harder test: we re-ran the entire selection blind — the optimizer allowed to see only that earliest quarter, its choices then frozen and marched across the unseen remainder. The blind committee overlaps the production ensemble ten times more than chance, and it finishes the unseen stretch positive, with a win-rate four sigma above coin flip. Smaller and rougher than the production system, as it should be — it saw a quarter of the evidence — but the direction is the point: the procedure finds the same vein without seeing the future.

None of this makes selection risk zero; multiplicity is a tax one discloses, not a sin one hides [1][2]. It is why the composition was frozen before the current live stretch began, and why the only exam we present without an asterisk is the one that accumulates from here forward, in public, one timestamped call at a time.

Method notes: temperament features are computed from call metadata only (frequency, inter-call rhythm, early precision); AUCs are member-vs-pool discrimination on the screening window. The blind re-selection uses the production optimizer and objective, restricted to the screening window.

REFERENCES
  1. Bailey, D., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., Zhu, Q. “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting.” Journal of Computational Finance, 2017.
  2. Harvey, C., Liu, Y., Zhu, H. “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns.” Review of Financial Studies, 2016.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 15

You cannot simply cut the bad neurons out

SUPERPOSITION · POLYSEMANTIC UNITS · ERROR SIGNATURES · GATES OVER SCALPELS

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

Watch information move through one of our experts and the temptation is immediate. Twenty-second tokens enter at the bottom; the first convolutional layers learn a micro-grammar — a lifted offer, a leaning book, a silence that is not empty; each layer widens the span of time a unit can see, so mid-network units respond to phrases — absorption, exhaustion, the drumbeat of one-sided aggression — and the deepest layers hold whole sentences of regime. Somewhere in that hierarchy live the units that fire before the model’s worst calls. Why not find them and cut them out?

Because in a trained network, concepts do not get private neurons. Interpretability research calls it superposition: a network representing more features than it has units stores them in overlapping combinations, and a single unit ends up polysemantic — carrying a fragment of “trend exhaustion” entangled with a fragment of “healthy pullback” [1][2]. Ablate the unit that misfires in crashes and you also lobotomize a talent that pays elsewhere. Surgery on shared weights is not removal; it is untangling — and untangling is the open research problem of the field.

So the lab took the other road, the one causal-tracing work points toward [3]: do not cut the memory — learn to hear when it is speaking. Errors, it turns out, have an internal signature. The clearest one we have published: when every prediction horizon of a model agrees at once — full unanimity, maximal apparent confidence — accuracy collapses below a coin flip. Unanimity is what self-deception looks like from inside. Signatures like that become gates: states in which the system is required to stay silent, with the entity left whole, scars and all.

This is also, quietly, the deepest argument for the ensemble in the previous note: seventy differently-aged snapshots do not share one blind spot, and the consensus requirement is itself a gate — built not from one network’s self-report, but from the disagreement of many.

Method notes: layer-span arithmetic and the unanimity signature are measured on our production experts; per-unit attributions are exploratory, and we will publish them the day they replicate. No claim is made that individual market concepts are localized — the evidence points the other way.

REFERENCES
  1. Elhage, N. et al. “Toy Models of Superposition.” Anthropic, 2022.
  2. Olah, C. et al. “Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits.” Distill, 2020.
  3. Meng, K. et al. “Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT.” NeurIPS, 2022.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 16

Where the volatility went: notes toward the next instruments

BTC REALIZED VOL ≈ HALVED SINCE 2021 · LIQUID ALTS AT 88–101% · THE PIPELINE IS TICKER-AGNOSTIC

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

A first-touch system is a hunter of movement: a call can score only when price travels. So the macro fact that shapes our roadmap is simple to state — Bitcoin’s realized volatility has roughly halved since 2021, with recent annualized medians near 40%, while the liquid altcoin universe still breathes at 88–101%. On the public track you can see what a quieter ocean does to a hunter: the system’s only meaningful loss regime is not being wrong — direction was fatally wrong in a low single-digit share of trades — but running out of clock when the market refuses to move.

The instrument, then, is a parameter — and by design, so is our pipeline. The collectors, the token language, the walk-forward gauntlet, the trade-level judge: all of it transfers to another perpetual by changing a ticker, not an architecture. What does not transfer for free is the two things we will measure before believing: microstructure costs (thinner books tax a simulator harder than any hit-rate flatters it) and the crowd itself — each instrument’s flow has its own dialect, and experts will be retrained natively, not transplanted.

The same discipline that built this track applies to its expansion: no instrument joins the public dashboard until it has walked its own gauntlet — its own reserve of untouched history, its own trade-level audit, its own selection alibi. Markets with double the breathing room are an opportunity; they are not an excuse to lower the bar. When the next track appears here, it will arrive the way this one did — with its scars published on day one.

Method notes: volatility figures are realized, annualized medians over multi-year windows across a 60+ perpetual universe. Instrument selection will be published together with its own gauntlet, the day its untouched reserve has matured — the same order of ceremony this track followed.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 01

The gauntlet, week by week

FROZEN CHECKPOINT · 56 CONSECUTIVE WALK-FORWARD WEEKS · CONVICTION ≥ 0.90 · INDEPENDENT PRICE RECORD

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

Before a single prediction went public, the production checkpoint walked fifty-six consecutive weeks of history beyond its training — June 2025 through mid-July 2026, no gaps, no re-picks. Each week it was asked the same question: commit only where conviction clears 0.90, and let first-touch decide — does price travel at least around a hundred basis points your way before it travels that far against you? Grading is automatic, against an independent, continuous price record.

The first thing the record shows is silence. In 22 of 56 weeks the model produced not a single call at the 0.90 gate. That is not downtime — it is the conviction gate doing its work: no geometry it trusts, no call. A public track that never goes quiet should worry you.

The second is what conviction buys. When it does speak, the tape is extreme in both directions. Twelve separate weeks landed at a 100% hit-rate (from quiet 2-call weeks to c43 with 57 calls); the densest week of the record, c69, fired 359 calls and hit 99.2% of them. Across all 56 weeks the model committed to 3,164 high-conviction calls.

The third is the temper, published in full. Some weeks the same conviction inverts: c27 and c37 went to 0% (26 and 55 calls), c55 hit 2.9% of 102, c73 8.9%, c80 — the newest week on the track — 15.2%. These are regime breaks, and they stay on the record with the same weight as the perfect weeks. A model whose failure mode is mapped — wrong together, not wrong randomly — is a model whose failures can be studied rather than merely suffered.

Why weekly walk-forward, and not one big backtest

A single aggregated backtest yields a single number — and a number that flatters easily: selection across configurations quietly inflates it, a problem formalized as backtest overfitting and data snooping in the quantitative-finance literature [1][2][3]. A week-by-week gauntlet publishes the distribution instead of the summary: every regime the market offered in thirteen months gets its own verdict, and variance — the thing a summary hides — becomes the headline. This is also the honest way to live with non-stationarity: concept-drift research has long argued that models on drifting streams must be evaluated as sequences of local exams, not one global average [4], and adaptive-markets theory expects edges to breathe and rotate rather than persist uniformly [5].

What the distribution reveals

The tape has a specific texture: silence, near-perfect bursts, and occasional coherent inversion. Each is a property of the model, not noise around an average. Silence is abstention — no structure it trusts, no call. Bursts are conviction concentrated in a few stretches. Coherent inversion — wrong together, on regime breaks — is detectable in real time precisely because it is coherent: a short streak of high-conviction misses is informative in a way scattered noise is not, and can trip a circuit-breaker. None of this is visible in a single aggregate number; all of it falls out of the weekly form.

Limitations

Fifty-six weeks samples regimes richly and tail events sparsely — which is exactly why this track keeps growing in public rather than ending at a flattering cut-off. Hit-rates are measured before any cost of acting on them, by design (per-call passports on the dashboard carry realized basis points for anyone’s cost model), and call counts are model-native tokens above the gate — the raw form, published because raw is the one form that cannot be curated.

Method notes: weeks c74, c75 and c78 are reported under the repaired judge (see “We audited our own judge”); the frozen checkpoint, its normalizer and the conviction gate are identical across all 56 weeks and are fingerprinted by checksum in the release contract. Call counts are model-native (20-second cadence tokens above gate), which is why they exceed the deduplicated dots shown on the dashboard preview.

REFERENCES
  1. White, H. “A Reality Check for Data Snooping.” Econometrica, 2000.
  2. Bailey, D., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., Zhu, Q. “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting.” Journal of Computational Finance, 2017.
  3. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
  4. Gama, J. et al. “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation.” ACM Computing Surveys, 2014.
  5. Lo, A. “The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2004.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 02

We audited our own judge — and it cost us three perfect weeks

22 WEEKS RE-JUDGED · 19 UNCHANGED TO THE DECIMAL · 3 CORRECTED DOWNWARD

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

The judge in this lab is a separate, continuous price record: predictions are graded against it automatically, and we never mark our own exam. In July we found a flaw — not in the model, in the judge. On a handful of stretches the judge’s price feed had gaps that its loader rendered as flat, motionless bands. A prediction graded against a flat band can look brilliant for free.

It was a human eye on the public chart that caught it: clusters of “perfect” arrows sitting on suspiciously frozen price. We rebuilt the judge on an unbroken feed and re-graded every affected week of the live tail — all twenty-two of them, no exceptions.

Nineteen weeks did not move by more than rounding. Three fell, hard: one week dropped from 96.2% to 46.2% hit-rate, another from 92.4% to 75.4%, a third from 74.6% to 70.7%. Every number this lab publishes today — including the heatmap in the previous note — is the corrected, harder one.

We could have quietly kept the flattering numbers; the flaw was in nobody’s favour but ours. We prefer the other trade: a stricter judge is worth more than a prettier record, because every future number inherits its credibility. The gaps themselves also taught us something operational — the lab now runs its own uninterrupted collection of the judging feed, with checksum parity against a second source, so a flat band cannot impersonate a market again.

Data quality is part of the model

Machine-learning practice has a well-documented blind spot: effort concentrates on models while the data infrastructure that grades and feeds them decays quietly — “data cascades,” as the human-centered AI literature names the phenomenon [1]. A grading feed is an instrument, and an instrument has failure modes of its own. A flat band born from a gap is a particularly vicious one: it does not look like an error, it looks like calm — and calm is exactly what a barrier-based judge rewards. In the taxonomy of label problems this is silent, systematic label corruption: invisible to aggregate statistics, correlated with exactly the moments when data pipelines strain [2].

The economics of a stricter judge

The audit was voluntary in the narrow sense — no external party would have caught it, because the raw feeds are commercial and the reconstruction is ours. That is precisely why it had to happen: a published record inherits the credibility of its weakest instrument, and any number that can be flattered by infrastructure eventually will be, if only by accident [3]. Trading three perfect-looking weeks for a judge that can no longer be fooled is, in expectation, the cheapest credibility this lab will ever buy. The repaired pipeline now enforces what the flaw taught: continuous independent collection of the judging feed, checksum parity against a second source, and a hard rule that gaps grade as ungradable, not as stillness.

Limitations

The audit re-graded the 22-week live tail where the affected feed was in use; earlier weeks were graded from a different reconstruction lineage and matched the repaired judge where cross-checked. The audit corrects grading only — it neither improves nor degrades the model, and post-audit numbers remain measured before any cost of acting on them.

Method notes: the checkpoint, gate and normalizer were untouched by the audit — only the grading record changed. The pre-audit and post-audit gradings are both archived; the deltas above are reproducible from the frozen dumps.

REFERENCES
  1. Sambasivan, N. et al. “‘Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work’: Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI.” CHI, 2021.
  2. Frénay, B., Verleysen, M. “Classification in the Presence of Label Noise: a Survey.” IEEE TNNLS, 2014.
  3. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 03

Same mind, different ears: surviving a data-provider migration

ONE FROZEN CHECKPOINT · TWO INDEPENDENT RAW FEEDS · 22 SHARED SPEAKING WEEKS · 22/22 SAME SIDE OF CHANCE

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Every model in this lab eats the market through a feature language computed from raw microstructure. That language was designed to describe structure, not the fingerprint of any one data vendor. In July we ran the strongest test of that claim we know: the same frozen checkpoint, fed the same weeks of history rebuilt from two completely independent raw sources — different collection stacks, different outage patterns, different microstructure quirks.

The two ears do not hear identically — and that is the honest part. Call counts differ (one feed is denser and speaks in a few weeks where the other stays silent), and magnitudes wobble: one week grades 77% on feed A and 95% on feed B. But across every week where both feeds speak, the verdict lands on the same side of chance — 22 of 22 — and the catastrophic weeks are catastrophic in both. The model’s opinion of the market survives a change of ears; only the sharpness of hearing shifts.

This is also why the lab now runs its own uninterrupted raw collection in parallel with commercial feeds: not because any vendor failed us, but because the migration test taught us that independence of the input path is a property you can measure — and therefore one you can keep re-verifying rather than assume.

Robustness as an invariance test

The experiment belongs to a family the literature calls dataset-shift and invariance testing [1][2]: hold the mechanism fixed, vary a nuisance factor that should not matter, and measure what leaks through. Here the nuisance factor is the entire acquisition path — collector, transport, outage profile, vendor quirks. The feature language acts as an abstraction barrier: if the model’s verdicts survive the swap, the representation has captured market structure rather than vendor texture. Verdicts surviving 22-of-22 on the side of chance — while call density visibly shifts — is the signature of exactly that: the invariant part of the signal lives above the vendor layer, and the vendor layer contributes sensitivity, not opinion.

What did not survive: hearing

Densities differ — one feed produces more above-gate calls, and in six weeks exactly one of the two feeds speaks while the other stays silent. This is worth publishing because it bounds the claim honestly: the language is invariant in direction, not in sensitivity. Operationally that bound converted into policy: the lab’s own uninterrupted collection now runs in parallel with commercial feeds, with checksum parity between sources — migration is a measured invariance, re-verified continuously rather than assumed [3].

Limitations

The test is deliberately scoped: one deep venue — the market this lab is built around — and side-of-chance agreement as the decision-relevant equivalence (per-week magnitudes wobble; verdicts do not). Silence asymmetries are reported, not hidden, because they are the honest price of independent ears. Breadth across venues is a roadmap item, not an apology.

Method notes: identical checkpoint, gate and normalizer lineage across both runs; feeds rebuilt into the same feature schema by the same pipeline. Vendor names are omitted — the result is about the language, not the vendor.

REFERENCES
  1. Quiñonero-Candela, J. et al. (eds.) Dataset Shift in Machine Learning. MIT Press, 2009.
  2. Peters, J., Bühlmann, P., Meinshausen, N. “Causal Inference by Using Invariant Prediction.” JRSS-B, 2016.
  3. Gama, J. et al. “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation.” ACM Computing Surveys, 2014.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 04

The architecture races: what capacity does and does not buy

CONTROLLED SLICE · EQUAL DATA · EQUAL BUDGET · ONLY THE NETWORK CHANGES

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Behind the public checkpoint sits a zoo. Over the project’s life we raced candidate families spanning three orders of magnitude in parameter count — compact temporal families, recurrent stacks, sequence-attention hybrids, test-time-memory designs inspired by the Titans line of work, selective state-space variants — all on equal data, judged by the same walk-forward exam. Below is one controlled slice: a single hard validation week, a single feature diet, only the network family and its size changing.

Capacity is not monotonic here. The compact network wins the week; twenty times more parameters roughly matches it; forty times more loses ground; at ×175 the plain-trained giant slides toward chance — and only a flat-minima optimizer variant pulls it back to parity. On non-stationary market data, the data-to-parameter ratio writes its own law: past a threshold, extra capacity memorizes regimes instead of learning structure.

Attention did not win this fight either. The sequence-attention candidate — the family that dominates language — lands mid-pack on equal data. We read this not as “attention is weak” but as a statement about regime density: a market week simply does not offer the token volume that attention’s appetite is built for. The production family was chosen the boring way: by surviving more weeks of the gauntlet than anything else, at a size the data can feed.

Scaling laws meet non-stationary data

Language-model scaling laws teach that capacity must be fed: performance scales predictably only when parameters and data grow together, and compute-optimal training wants far more tokens per parameter than early practice assumed [1][2]. Market data breaks the recipe in a specific way: the binding constraint is not raw token count but regime count. A year of 20-second cadence supplies millions of windows drawn from only a handful of statistically distinct market regimes — the effective sample, in the sense that matters for generalization, is orders of magnitude smaller than the token count suggests. That is our reading of the ladder above: past the point where capacity exhausts the regime diversity, additional parameters buy memorization of particular regimes, which walk-forward exams then punish [3]. The attention result reads the same way: the family whose dominance was established at web-scale token counts [4] lands mid-pack when the effective sample is regime-limited.

Flat minima, and why only the giant needed them

The one intervention that rescued the ×175 candidate — an optimizer that prefers flat regions of the loss surface [5] — is itself an old idea: flat minima were proposed as a generalization principle decades before deep learning’s current era [6]. The interaction is the interesting part: the compact network showed no comparable benefit. Under the regime-scarcity reading this is expected — sharp minima are where an over-parameterized network stores regime-specific detail, so flatness constrains precisely the failure mode that excess capacity enables. Flat-minima optimization, in this lab’s experience, is a capacity tax paid only where capacity exceeds the data’s effective richness.

Limitations

The slice is deliberately narrow, and that is its function: a single hard validation window under equal treatment is a disqualifier, not a leaderboard. Families that cannot clear a hard week under identical data and budget do not earn wider exams; families that do were re-raced across the full week-by-week gauntlet before any production decision. The metric is the harness’s directional score, not deployment PnL, and the Titans-inspired and state-space families [7][8] were raced in earlier eras on different stands, so they appear here qualitatively only.

Method notes: all runs share data window, feature schema, label definition and training budget; scores are the harness’s primary directional validation metric for the same week. Families are named at the level of the family; the Titans-inspired and state-space families were raced in earlier eras on different stands and are reported qualitatively only.

LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 05 · FROM THE ARCHIVE

When generalization arrives late: the run that taught us checkpoint governance

61 EPOCHS · DETERMINISTIC SEED · VALIDATION PEAK 30 EPOCHS AFTER THE “CORRECT” EARLY STOP

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: its lesson carries into AXIOM 5.1, which takes it to its end — no checkpoint selection at all (note 25).

Long before the current system, in an archived late-2025 experiment on a small daily-granularity dataset, we let a training run go far past every textbook stopping rule — and watched something that changed how this lab treats checkpoints ever since.

By every loss-based rule the run was overfitting from epoch six onward. Yet the best generalization of the entire run arrived at epoch 37 — an abrupt, isolated peak, stable in its timing under the fixed seed, long after the loss curve had said goodbye. The mechanistic-interpretability literature calls the extreme version of this grokking: internal circuits keep reorganizing beneath a surface that looks like pure memorization, until generalization surfaces late [1][2]. Our run is that phenomenon’s cousin on noisy financial data, published for its timing, not its magnitude.

The lesson stuck. If generalization can arrive out of sync with the loss, then a single “best checkpoint by loss” is a gamble. The production system that followed treats checkpoints as a population: every candidate faces the full week-by-week gauntlet, selection happens on out-of-sample behaviour across many weeks, and the final choice is governed by stability, not by a single scalar. The silent weeks and the temper you see on the public track are downstream of a rule this old run wrote for us: never let one curve pick your model.

Relation to the grokking literature

Delayed generalization has a name and a growing literature. Grokking was first documented on small algorithmic datasets: networks that memorize completely, then — long after — snap into perfect generalization [1]. Mechanistic follow-ups showed the delay is not magic: internal circuits form progressively, and hidden progress measures rise before any external metric moves [2]. The broader lesson generalizes past the toy settings: train-metric, validation-loss and validation-accuracy are three different instruments that can disagree for extended stretches — the same decoupling that double-descent phenomena exhibit along the capacity axis [3][4]. Our archive run is a noisy-data cousin of the family: no clean phase transition, but an unambiguous, seed-stable peak of generalization arriving thirty-two epochs after the loss-based verdict, on data where the textbook rule would have frozen the worse model.

From anecdote to protocol

The operational consequence outgrew the anecdote. If generalization can arrive out of sync with the loss, checkpoint selection is a multiple-testing problem over a population of candidates — and selection by a single scalar is exactly the overfitting-by-selection that the backtest literature warns about [5]. The production protocol that descends from this run treats checkpoints as a population: candidates are dumped on a fixed cadence, every candidate faces the same week-by-week walk-forward gauntlet, and promotion is decided by stability of out-of-sample behaviour across weeks — not by the training curve. The public checkpoint of that era was chosen by that gauntlet, over rivals with prettier losses.

Limitations

This is archaeology, and we treat it with an archaeologist’s discipline: the era’s validation slice was small, so the peak’s magnitude is anecdote — we quote it with its uncertainty (±7 points at two sigma) and rest nothing on it. What the artifact proves is about instruments: loss and generalization can disagree for thirty epochs, and any selection rule blind to that will freeze the wrong model. The production protocol descended from this run; the run itself stays in the museum.

Method notes: archive run, November 2025, deterministic seed, small daily-granularity dataset from a pre-production era; preserved logs are reproducible end-to-end. Reported for its methodological consequence, not as evidence of skill.

REFERENCES
  1. Power, A. et al. “Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets.” arXiv:2201.02177, 2022.
  2. Nanda, N. et al. “Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability.” ICLR, 2023.
  3. Belkin, M. et al. “Reconciling Modern Machine-Learning Practice and the Classical Bias–Variance Trade-off.” PNAS, 2019.
  4. Nakkiran, P. et al. “Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt.” ICLR, 2020.
  5. Bailey, D. et al. “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting.” Journal of Computational Finance, 2017.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 06

Memory, not skill: what an LLM’s tenfold backtest really proved

SIX HARNESS GENERATIONS · FRONTIER LLM TRADERS · ONE CONTROLLED DISGUISE EXPERIMENT

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

The benchmarks section of this site shows the headline: frontier language models, seated in honest cursor-forward harnesses, converge to a coin flip on anonymized market data — while one non-anonymized run grew its simulator score more than tenfold. This note is the story of how we proved why.

The suspicion. The tenfold run knew the asset and the calendar. Its decision log read like a historian’s diary — citing macro events by name before “discovering” them in the tape, shorting into levels it described as historically impassable. Asked directly, the model acknowledged leaning on its knowledge of that era rather than on the live tape. Impressive numbers; compromised experiment.

The controlled test. We re-ran the same model on the same market window with one variable changed: the disguise. Identified — real names, real dates — it hit 67.7% of its calls. Anonymized — relative prices, neutral clock, no names — the same mind on the same week fell to 52.9%: statistically, a coin. The fifteen-point gap is the measured value of remembering the era.

The canary ladder. To make anonymization testable rather than aspirational, we built recognition canaries: before any backtest is trusted, a probe asks the model to identify the asset and era from the data alone. Raw absolute prices light the canary instantly (the model names the asset with high confidence); after multiplicative rescaling it drifts to generic guesses; full anonymization leaves it blind. And one inverse experiment sealed the case: asked to deliberately score below chance on anonymized data by inverting its own intuition, the model could not do it reliably — there was no stable skill to invert.

Why we publish this. Every claim that a language model can predict a market must clear this bar: if the model can name the year, it is reciting, not reading. Our specialized models are trained and examined on the other side of that bar — walk-forward, on data that postdates every weight — which is the only regime where the word “skill” means anything.

Contamination is the default, not the exception

Large language models memorize verbatim slices of their training corpora, and that memorization is extractable and quantifiable [1][2]; benchmark contamination — evaluation data leaking into training — is pervasive enough to have its own literature of detection and exploitation [3]. A financial backtest on a public asset’s public past is the worst case of that phenomenon dressed as an experiment: the “test set” is one of the most heavily discussed time series in the model’s training distribution — prices, narratives, dates, outcomes. In that light our tenfold run is not an anomaly to explain away; it is the expected behaviour of a well-trained language model handed its own memories and a scoreboard.

Designing disguises that can be audited

The methodological contribution we care about is not the anonymization itself but making it testable. Recognition canaries turn “the data is anonymized” from an assertion into a measurement: probe the model to identify asset and era from the data alone, before any result is trusted — a spiritual cousin of membership-inference auditing [4]. The ladder behaved like an instrument should: raw absolute prices → confident identification; multiplicative rescaling → generic guesses; full disguise → blindness. Only behind a blind canary does a coin-flip result become interpretable as absence of skill rather than absence of memory.

Why specialized models sit on the other side of this bar

The specialized network cannot recite its exam: its public track postdates every weight by construction, and its inputs are microstructure tokens, not narratives. Walk-forward time is the one axis that cannot be contaminated — the future is absent from every training corpus. That asymmetry, more than any architecture choice, is what separates “reading the tape” from “remembering the year,” and it is why every claim this lab publishes is anchored to post-cutoff, continuously growing history.

Limitations

The disguise pair is a single-variable experiment by design — one model family, one window, one changed condition — because single-variable is the only design that isolates memory. Its anonymized leg carried a book-reconstruction defect we flagged at the time, so the pair is labelled diagnostic and its fifteen-point gap is quoted as measurement, not monument. Harness generations varied in cost and bracket settings; cross-generation multiples are therefore indicative — the within-generation contrasts are the evidence.

Method notes: harness generations varied in costs and bracket geometry (5–30 bps, several bracket widths); the disguise comparison is same-model, same-window, single-variable. The identified run’s ledger, the recognition probes and the inversion run are archived in full.

REFERENCES

  2. Carlini, N. et al. “Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models.” ICLR, 2023.
  3. Magar, I., Schwartz, R. “Data Contamination: From Memorization to Exploitation.” ACL, 2022.
  4. Shokri, R. et al. “Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models.” IEEE S&P, 2017.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 07

Market as a language: tokenizing raw order flow for sequence models

EVENT-TIME TOKENS · A MICROSTRUCTURE VOCABULARY · ONE LAW: NOT A SINGLE BIT FROM THE FUTURE

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Every domain that deep learning has conquered was first made speakable: text became subword tokens [1], raw audio became sample streams a network could voice [2], proteins became residue sequences [3]. Markets have resisted not because they lack structure but because the field keeps handing models the wrong sentences — hourly candles, daily closes, indicators averaged into mush. The information that decides the next hundred basis points lives in the microstructure: who lifted the offer, how the book leaned, how aggression clustered. Our first design decision was therefore linguistic, not architectural: define the token before you argue about the network.

The clock problem

Calendar time is the wrong clock for markets: an hour of Sunday drift and an hour of cascade carry incomparable amounts of event. Market-microstructure research has long argued for event-driven clocks — volume clocks, information-driven bars — that sample activity, not wall time [4][5]. Our cadence is a compromise struck deliberately fine: fast enough that bursts do not smear into averages, slow enough that a multi-year corpus stays trainable end-to-end. At that cadence a year of one market is millions of tokens — a corpus, not a spreadsheet.

What a token must contain

A token in our language is not a price — it is a paragraph: hundreds of engineered features describing that slice’s trades, quotes and book posture across several nested granularities, each feature designed to survive two filters. First, structure over identity: features describe relations (imbalances, intensities, relative displacements), not absolute levels that would let a model memorize eras — the same discipline our anonymization canaries enforce on LLM benchmarks. Second, vendor independence: the language survived a full data-provider migration with verdicts intact, which is the strongest evidence we have that it encodes market structure rather than feed texture.

The lookahead law

The quiet killer of financial ML is information from the future leaking into the past — through labels, through normalization, through joins [5]. In this lab the law is absolute and mechanical: every pipeline stage is gated, normalization statistics are fitted strictly on data preceding the point of use, labels are resolved by first-touch against a separate continuous record, and any build whose fingerprints disagree with the accepted lineage refuses to publish itself. Two of this journal’s first six notes exist because those gates fired in anger.

Limitations

The vocabulary was designed for one deep, liquid, always-open market; its transfer to thinner venues is an open research question, not a claim. And a language is only as honest as its corpus: our tick-level history is institutional-grade, but pre-2021 depth data carries vendor reconstruction artifacts we treat as second-class evidence.

REFERENCES
  1. Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., Birch, A. “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units.” ACL, 2016.
  2. van den Oord, A. et al. “WaveNet: A Generative Model for Raw Audio.” arXiv:1609.03499, 2016.
  3. Jumper, J. et al. “Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold.” Nature, 2021.
  4. Easley, D., López de Prado, M., O’Hara, M. “The Volume Clock: Insights into the High-Frequency Paradigm.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2012.
  5. López de Prado, M. Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley, 2018.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 08

Why our model misses at reversals: the anatomy of an inversion

SIX INVERTED WEEKS IN 56 · ERRORS THAT ARRIVE TOGETHER · AN OPEN PROBLEM WE PUBLISH ANYWAY

WRITTEN IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAThe committee-of-experts system described here is the direct ancestor of today’s weekly-reborn reader. Its figures — and its simulators, frames and gates — belong to that era’s exam, preserved exactly as filed; the record above answers only to the symmetric ±1% first-touch.

The gauntlet note shows the phenomenon; this note stares at it. In six of fifty-six walk-forward weeks the model’s high-conviction calls did not merely miss — they inverted: c27 hit 0% of 26 calls, c37 0% of 55, c55 2.9% of 102, c73 8.9%, c77 12.1%, c80 15.2%. Numbers that far below chance are not noise. A coin cannot score 3% on a hundred flips; only a model with a consistent opinion, consistently wrong, can.

Wrong together is information

Decompose any of those weeks and the errors share a fingerprint: they cluster in time, they lean the same direction, and they sit at structural turning points — exactly where the model’s timing gift concentrates its calls. The picture is of a mind reading the location of the decisive moment correctly and the resolution of that moment backwards: geometry that historically broke one way breaking, that week, the other. In drift language, these are abrupt regime transitions rather than gradual drift [1]; in adaptive-markets language, weeks where the prevailing strategy population flipped the payoff of the pattern [2].

Why we have not “fixed” it

The tempting patch — detect an inversion week early and flip the sign — is a trap we have so far declined: a sign-flipping wrapper is a second model with its own failure modes, and trained on six positive examples it would be statistical fiction [3]. The honest state of knowledge is: the trigger conditions are not yet predictable ex-ante with the evidence we hold, coherence makes inversion detectable within days ex-post, and that detectability is already useful even while the mechanism remains open. We publish the phenomenon precisely because it is unsolved — it is the sharpest research question this track has produced, and the reason the lab reads latent spaces, not just scoreboards.

Limitations

Six events is a small sample of a rare mode; per-week error decompositions are internal (they lean on unpublished feature diagnostics); and nothing here should read as a promise that inversion frequency is stationary — that question is exactly what the growing track exists to answer.

Method notes: weekly figures are from the frozen per-token dumps under the repaired judge; “coherence” claims are qualitative summaries of internal decompositions.

REFERENCES
  1. Gama, J. et al. “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation.” ACM Computing Surveys, 2014.
  2. Lo, A. “The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis.” Journal of Portfolio Management, 2004.
  3. Bailey, D. et al. “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting.” Journal of Computational Finance, 2017.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 09 · POSITION

Synthetic order flow via next-token generation — and why we keep it in the lab

A GENERATIVE RESEARCH THREAD · DELIBERATELY UNRELEASED

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

If a network can read the market’s language, a sibling network can learn to speak it: generate plausible order-flow continuations token by token, the way language models generate text. The appeal for a data-limited field is obvious — markets offer few truly distinct regimes, and a faithful generator would be a regime factory: synthetic crashes to stress-test the reader, counterfactual weeks to widen the exam, augmentation for the rare modes (inversions above all) that real history undersamples.

We run this thread — and we deliberately do not deploy it into training. The reason is the snowball. A generator trained on the market’s past, feeding a predictor whose behaviour we then study, creates a closed loop in which the predictor’s strengths and blind spots are quietly re-imprinted and amplified; the generative-model literature now documents how models trained on model output degrade — distributions narrow, tails vanish, rare modes die first [1]. In markets the tails are the point: a synthetic corpus that undersamples the improbable would teach precisely the wrong lesson at precisely the decisive moments. Until we can certify tail fidelity against held-out real extremes — a measurement problem we consider unsolved, here and in the field [2] — the generator stays a laboratory instrument: a stress-tester and a hypothesis engine, not a teacher.

Method notes: this is a research position, not a result; no synthetic data has contributed to any training corpus behind the public track.

REFERENCES
  1. Shumailov, I. et al. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature, 2024.
  2. Assefa, S. et al. “Generating Synthetic Data in Finance: Opportunities, Challenges and Pitfalls.” ACM ICAIF, 2020.
LANIAKEA LAB NOTES · NO. 10

The optimizer is an epistemology: a flat-minima bake-off

FIVE TRAINING RECIPES · ONE NETWORK · ONE EXAM · PAPER EFFECTS, REPRODUCED AND BOUNDED

FILED IN THE GENERATION 1–2 ERAKept because it earned it: the method and its lessons carry into AXIOM 5.1 unchanged.

Two networks with identical architecture and identical data can hold different kinds of beliefs, because the optimizer decides which minima are reachable — and minima have character. Sharp basins store detail; flat basins store structure that survives perturbation, a connection conjectured decades ago [1] and made practical by sharpness-aware training [2][3]. On a non-stationary market, where next week is always a perturbation of last week, that distinction stops being philosophy and becomes method. So we ran the bake-off properly: same network family, same feature diet, same walk-forward exam — five training recipes in the ring: an adaptive-moment baseline, sharpness-aware minimization, its adaptive variant, and two learning-rate regimes — a conventional cosine decay and a deliberately hot schedule held high before stepped drops.

What reproduced from the papers

Three published promises survived contact with market data, and they are the reason this note exists. Calibration: flat-minima training measurably tightened the conviction tail — the model’s stated confidence tracked its realized hit-rate more faithfully, the failure mode where the top confidence bucket quietly turns toxic softened; on a system whose public gate is a confidence threshold, calibration is substance, not cosmetics [4]. Stability across weeks: the highest-conviction bucket held its advantage across more consecutive walk-forward weeks under sharpness-aware variants — flatness bought week-to-week persistence, exactly the currency a gauntlet pays in. Capacity rescue: as the architecture-races note shows, the ×175 giant moved from near-chance to parity under a flat-minima recipe while the compact winner barely responded — sharpness constraints tax precisely the failure mode that excess capacity enables.

What flatness did not buy

The bake-off also drew a hard boundary, and we publish the boundary with the wins: no optimizer rescued a cold regime. Weeks where the market’s geometry genuinely shifted stayed cold under every recipe — flat minima change how faithfully a model knows what it knows; they do not change what there is to know. And the learning-rate result cut the textbook way in half: the conventional decay schedule, praised for smooth convergence, doubled as an overfitting sink on this data — while the hot schedule behaved as an implicit regularizer, slowing the slide into overconfidence that our per-epoch dumps make visible [5][6]. Optimization choices, it turns out, are among the quietest safeguards in the stack.

This door was opened by an insight from our work with the latest Claude models. Reading our per-epoch confidence dumps with us, Claude recognized the signature of sharp-basin overfitting in the way conviction curdled late in training, connected it to the flat-minima literature and proposed the sharpness-aware family as the corrective; the bake-off that tested the idea was designed in the same collaboration: five candidates instrumented rollback-safe, per-epoch distribution dumps for every run, every claim settled by the same week-by-week exam that judges the models. Customization at this depth — optimizer surgery, custom schedules, custom kernels — became routine for a lab of our size once that kind of collaboration was available on demand.

Limitations

Which recipe ships in production, and at what sharpness radius, is not reported here. Effects reported here are directional summaries across tested cycles of one network family at one feature scale; the boundary claim (“no regime rescue”) is the most replicated result in our archive, observed independently across eras, and it stands.

Method notes: all five recipes shared network family, data diet, schedule length and evaluation protocol; per-epoch confidence-distribution dumps and per-week bucket tapes are archived for every run cited.

REFERENCES

  3. Kwon, J. et al. “ASAM: Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Scale-Invariant Learning.” ICML, 2021.
  4. Guo, C. et al. “On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks.” ICML, 2017.
